newsitem.title: GERMANY: German FDP defends its change on solidarity tax.
newsitem.headline: German FDP defends its change on solidarity tax.

text.p: Germany's junior coalition partner Free Democrats, struggling to salvage their tarnished reputation, at the weekend defended a government decision to postpone a planned tax cut to avoid an unpopular tax hike.

On Friday Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition government, in a bid to plug a seven billion mark gap in next year's budget, agreed to defer a one percentage point cut of the 7.5 percent solidarity tax planned for 1997.
The move threatens the Free Democrats' credibility, because the party survived this spring's round of regional elections largely on promises of future tax cuts.
Wolfgang Gerhard, head of the FDP, told an audience in Stuttgart "This was the only chance. Otherwise I would have had to justify a increase in taxes."
By postponing a cut in the solidarity tax, imposed to finance German unity, the government was able to prevent an equally unpopular increase in the petrol oil tax.
The Free Democrats scored a coup earlier in the year when it managed to convince its larger coalition partners to agree to a cut the solidarity tax next year.
Gerhard said his party would stick to plans to cut taxes further. "Tax increases would be counterproductive and would threaten everything that he hope to achieve in the coming years," he said.
Similarly CDU parliamentary leader Wolfgang Schaeuble told German radio "Reducing the burden on tax payers will continue to be the coalition's policy."
The Forsa research institute said only 16 percent of the population would have accepted a petrol tax increase while 33 percent would accept paying an unchanged solidarity tax.

Divisions however remain between the coalition partners with the FDP saying the solidarity tax should be cut by two percentage points in 1998 and the Kohl camp saying only that the reduction should be at least one percentage point.

The only point they seem to agree on is in putting all blame for the week's wrangling over taxation on the opposition Social Democrats who had threatened to use their upper house majority to block finance minister Theo Waigel's tax bill.
Mocking the scene, Joschka Fischer, head of the Greens, said monkeys acted more rationally than German politicians.
Similarly the Sueddeutsche Zeitung, in an editorial, worried that German politics were beginning to resemble an oriental bazaar rather than a solid, political stage.

While Waigel managed to fill part of the gap, another three billion marks still need to be found in other spending cuts. He promised however not to touch investments, which were necessary to prop up German economic recovery.

Waigel said the tax changes would not jeopardise his goal of reducing the budget deficit to 2.5 percent of economic output in 1997, below the three percent required to join the planned start of the single European currency in 1999.
"We will have no higher deficit," Waigel promised on Friday.
